title: Separated by our deeds
hookLine: separated by our own deeds, we ask the Lord in mercy to unite us (Barah Maha, ang 133)

lines: NO BIG FIGHT, JUST SMALL CHOICES.
cards: Two old friends stop talking. Nobody can quite remember when. There wasn't a big fight.
Just a missed call, a canceled plan, a comment taken the wrong way, a year of not reaching out. Each small choice made sense at the time.
Then one day you realize there's a distance between you that you built yourselves, one brick at a time.
Guru Arjan's Barah Maha begins exactly there: not with a month, but with how the distance got there, and who can close it.

teach.h: KIRAT KARAM: WHAT WE HAVE DONE.
teach.b: The opening stanza, on ang 133, in paraphrase: we are separated by the deeds we have done.
Have mercy, Lord, and unite us with yourself. Kirat karam ke veechhurhe. Kirat is what has been done; karam is action; veechhurhe, the separated ones, torn apart.
The stanza is honest about how it happened. Nobody else did it to us; our own doings built the distance. Yet the very next breath isn't despair.
It's a request: kar kirpaa, have mercy. Unite us. Then Guru Arjan paints the tiredness: wandering in the four corners and the ten directions, we've grown weary and come to your sanctuary.
And he reaches for two farm pictures every Punjabi listener would know. A cow that gives no milk is of no use.

teach.h: A COW WITHOUT MILK, A CROP WITHOUT WATER.
teach.b: A crop without water withers and won't fetch a price. Life without the One, he's saying, is like that: dry, unproductive, missing its whole point. Without meeting the beloved Friend, where can anyone find rest?
The homes and towns where the Beloved isn't present are like burning furnaces.

teach.h: OUR DEEDS, AND THE ONE'S GRACE.
teach.b: Each month to come will have its own color, but the root is here: separation by our own deeds, and a longing only grace can meet.
Notice the balance. The stanza doesn't excuse us; the distance is ours. But it doesn't ask us to close it alone, either.
In Sikh teaching, both are true at once: we're responsible for our deeds, and reunion comes by the One's grace.

how: Sikhs read the opening stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha before the months, and its plea for reunion is heard whenever the Barah Maha is sung or read on sangrand.

o: the lost ones, punished by an angry God
the wanderers who chose to leave home
the separated ones, torn apart by deeds

games.q: the opening stanza — tap the pairs.
p: of no use, like life without the One

s: the stanza blames someone else for the separation
it says we are separated by our own deeds.
the stanza asks the One for mercy and reunion
have mercy, and unite us with yourself.
the stanza says homes without the Beloved are like furnaces
the towns where the Beloved isn't present burn.

games.q: you've realized your own deeds built the distance between you and the One. what does the stanza do next?
o: give up; the distance is too great.
promise to close it alone by effort.
games.why: kirat karam ke veechhurhe, kar kirpaa: separated by our deeds, it asks the One in mercy to unite us.

practice: Think of one distance in your life you helped build, with a person, with a part of yourself or, if this is your language, with God, and without arguing whose fault it was, just admit your bricks.
Then let the opposite feeling come: a wish to close it. If you pray, hold the stanza's own request, kar kirpaa, have mercy; if you don't, simply hold the wish.

wordCard.voice: Veechhurhe, the separated ones, torn apart: the opening of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha says we are veechhurhe by what we've done, and ask the One in mercy to unite us.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: separated by the deeds we have done; the first line of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha.

carryVoice: Your line: unite us. It's a humble request, not a verdict. See you in the month of Chet.

sources.ref: Barah Maha, Majh M5, opening stanza, Ang 133
